newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Crude Outlook - sustaining a soft tone, for now.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Crude Outlook - sustaining a soft tone, for now.

text.p: U.S. crude prices are expected to sustain a soft tone this week ahead of an anticipated market turnaround pinned to renewed refinery demand, analysts said Monday.

Physical supplies from at home and abroad remain plentiful on the U.S. Gulf Coast, a fundamental trait that the market is not likely to shrug off quickly amid refinery run cuts in Europe and burgeoning output in the Atlantic Basin.

This extended bearish trend has prompted prices to flirt with contango, but most market-watchers don't expect prompt prices to exceed the forward month for more than a short period if at all, at least for now.

"I think the odds of (contango) are pretty good," said William Brown, president of W.H. Brown & Co in New York. "No way do I see the kind of backwardation that we saw in the second quarter of last year...But I think once the demand for crude turns up, we'll move back into modest backwardation."

John Saucer, an analyst with Smith Barney in Houston, was less convinced. "I think the opportunity for the market to go into contango may have come and gone...Next week, people are going to start buying."
The spread between April and May West Texas Intermediate/Cushing slipped in and out of slight contango late Monday morning, with April WTI around $21.00-10 a barrel.
Contango last hit the market very briefly in May 1995, but prolonged uncertainty over when Iraqi crude would re-enter the market sustained the backwardated trend, traders said.
Refiners emerging from planned maintenance are expected to begin shopping for crude in earnest in the second quarter to prepare for the summer driving season.
Although supplies are expected to remain abundant, this renewed demand should restore some balance to the market, analysts said.
Sour crude is likely to remain the weakest link in the physical chain, analysts said.
West Texas Sour/Midland was trading at a discount of around $2.80 a barrel to WTI/Cushing Monday morning, down 60 cents a barrel from a month ago.

Mounting availabilities from Venezuela, Mexico, the U.S. West Coast, the Gulf of Mexico, Canada and Iraq have undercut sour crudes, prompting sellers to adopt increasingly aggressive pricing strategies, traders said.
But the sweet-sour differential is expected to stabilize because of the relative weakness of sweet crudes and a natural correction as refiners shift gears, said Brown.
The spread between WTI and WTS has soared to $2.38 a barrel in February from just 79 cents a barrel a year earlier.
Sweets have come under pressure from a heavy influx of West African crude as well as some Brent cargoes from the North Sea.
Although the second quarter is likely to witness some recovery in crude prices, the outlook for late summer and autumn is cloudier.
"I'd be looking for prices around $18.00 or $19.00 in the third quarter," said Brown. "But I expect a lot of volatility this year."
